```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
required <- c("dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "sf", "readr", "scales", "jsonlite", "knitr")
missing <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) stop("Install missing packages: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
invisible(lapply(required, library, character.only = TRUE))
options(timeout = max(180, getOption("timeout")))
post_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE), mustWork = TRUE))
raw_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "data", "raw")
results_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "results")
fig_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "figures")
for (p in c(raw_dir, results_dir, fig_dir)) dir.create(p, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
source(file.path(post_dir, "scripts", "data.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())
source(file.path(post_dir, "scripts", "analysis.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())
state_borders <- shapes |> group_by(STATEFP) |> summarise(.groups = "drop")
```

**Do counties with relatively large manufacturing or business-services sectors also have higher household incomes?** An industry map can show where jobs are concentrated, but it cannot answer whether residents in those places have higher incomes. That requires comparing the employment pattern with household income in the same counties.

The answer depends on the sector. The median county income estimate is lower in the manufacturing-specialized group than in its comparison group, but higher in the business-services-specialized group. Two figures locate these groups and compare their incomes; neither result describes every county.

## What counts as specialization?

I use 2024 private-sector employment from [BLS QCEW](https://www.bls.gov/cew/additional-resources/open-data/csv-data-slices.htm) and [Census ACS household income](https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/groups/B19013.html) for the contiguous 48 states and Washington, DC. The income measure is the **2020–2024 five-year estimate in 2024 dollars**, not income observed only during 2024.

A county specializes in a sector here when that sector accounts for at least the same share of private jobs as it does nationally. The **location quotient**, or LQ, divides the county share by the U.S. share. For example, if a sector holds 20% of local jobs and 10% nationally, its LQ is 2. An LQ of 1 is the dividing line in the income comparison. I compare employment shares because raw job totals would mainly distinguish large counties from small ones.

## Where are the specialized counties?

```{r}
#| label: fig-specialization
#| fig-cap: "Private-sector employment concentration, 2024. Both panels use identical LQ classes; gray is unavailable, not zero. U.S. national benchmarks include all U.S. counties, while maps display the contiguous states and DC. Sources: BLS QCEW and Census 2024 cartographic boundaries; author calculations."
#| fig-alt: "Two county maps comparing manufacturing and professional/business-service location quotients, with a shared legend and state outlines."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
map_data <- shapes |> left_join(current, by = "GEOID")
p <- ggplot(map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = lq_band), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = state_borders, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = .18, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ sector, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c("#eff3ff", "#bdd7e7", "#4292c6", "#084594", "#bdbdbd"), lq_levels),
                    drop = FALSE, name = "Location quotient") +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(5070), datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Manufacturing and business services concentrate in different places") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
                                    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15))
save_figure(p, "figure1_specialization_maps.png", height = 9)
```

Figure 1 shows a manufacturing belt through the Midwest and Southeast. Business-services concentration is more scattered. The panels use the same categories, so darker shading means greater specialization in either sector. It does not mean more jobs in absolute terms: a small county can have a high LQ.

The map explains why I compare the sectors separately: their concentrations identify different sets of places, rather than one shared group of specialized counties. It also prevents a common reading mistake: large colored areas represent land, not large numbers of workers. Gray counties have unavailable employment information and are not counted as having no industry.

## Compare income in those same places

```{r}
#| label: fig-income
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of county median household income by 2024 sector concentration. Income is the ACS 2020–2024 five-year estimate, expressed in 2024 dollars. Each county has equal weight; boxes show the median and interquartile range, whiskers extend to 1.5 IQR, and points are outliers. This is not the distribution of individual household incomes. Sources: Census ACS and BLS QCEW."
#| fig-alt: "Two boxplot panels compare county median household incomes below versus at or above the national sector employment share. Each group shows its county count."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
p <- ggplot(income_sample, aes(concentration, income, fill = concentration)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .55, outlier.size = .6, outlier.alpha = .25) +
  geom_text(data = income_summary, aes(x = concentration, y = 0, label = paste0("n = ", n_counties)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ sector, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#bdd7e7", "#4292c6"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Below U.S.\nshare", "At/above U.S.\nshare")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = .001, suffix = "k"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(.03, .06))) +
  labs(title = "The income comparison differs by sector",
        x = NULL, y = "County median household income (2024 dollars)") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
save_figure(p, "figure2_income_comparison.png", height = 5.5)
```

Figure 2 separates counties with LQ below 1 from those with LQ at least 1, doing this separately for each sector. Each county receives equal weight. The line inside each box is the median of the **county income estimates**; the box covers the middle half of counties. It is not a distribution of individual households or industry wages.

Among manufacturing-specialized counties, the median county income estimate is **USD `r format(income_summary$median_income[income_summary$sector == 'Manufacturing' & income_summary$concentration == 'At/above U.S. share'], big.mark=',')`**, compared with **USD `r format(income_summary$median_income[income_summary$sector == 'Manufacturing' & income_summary$concentration == 'Below U.S. share'], big.mark=',')`** in the comparison group: **`r gap_text(income_gap('Manufacturing'))`**. For business services, the corresponding estimates are **USD `r format(income_summary$median_income[income_summary$sector == 'Professional/business services' & income_summary$concentration == 'At/above U.S. share'], big.mark=',')`** and **USD `r format(income_summary$median_income[income_summary$sector == 'Professional/business services' & income_summary$concentration == 'Below U.S. share'], big.mark=',')`**: **`r gap_text(income_gap('Professional/business services'))`**.

These opposite directions answer the question: the manufacturing comparison is negative, while the business-services comparison is positive. The boxes also overlap, so neither industry category tells us the income of every county within it.

## What this comparison leaves open

The figures show an association between places, not what an industry does to a particular household's income. QCEW counts jobs where people work; ACS measures households where people live. Commuting can separate those locations. Household income also includes sources other than wages, and the comparison does not adjust for education, household size, or local prices.

“Professional/business services” is also broader than professional occupations: it includes administrative support and waste services. Calling every county in that group a knowledge-job economy would misdescribe the data.

Employment disclosure limits leave different samples for the two sectors: `r sum(income_summary$n_counties[income_summary$sector == 'Manufacturing'])` manufacturing counties and `r sum(income_summary$n_counties[income_summary$sector == 'Professional/business services'])` business-services counties. Repeating the comparison on the same `r length(common_ids)` counties preserves both directions. Excluding imprecise income estimates does too. These checks reduce two specific concerns about the comparison; they do not establish causation or statistical significance.

## Takeaway

The map identifies industrial specialization; the income comparison tells a different story for each sector. Manufacturing concentration accompanies lower county income here, while business-services concentration accompanies higher income. Read an industry map as a description of local employment, then check residents' incomes directly before drawing conclusions about prosperity.

[Methods, saved data, sensitivity checks, and full source code](README.md) are documented with the [replication repository](https://github.com/Zhenxin-Li/Zhenxin-Li-website/tree/main/blog/posts/blog5).
